title: Hazel and the Archive
premise: Rosalind Fairweather, the colony's last xenolinguist, has spent nine years maintaining a beacon whose original purpose no record explains — and she no longer dreams in any human tongue. When the colony's children begin sharing one identical dream, Rosalind recognizes its structure as language: an invitation, or a warning, transmitted through the beacon she alone can read. Racing to the relay at the edge of dead space before the jump window closes, she must choose between loyalty to the found family that raised her and the truth that her arrival on this world was engineered by whatever speaks in the children's sleep. In the end she sends the answer the signal demands — sacrificing her own passage home — and the dreams stop, leaving the colony free and Rosalind forever changed, half-belonging to both worlds.
about_author: Mara Amberdale is the pen name of a former radio astronomer who spent six years at a remote listening post in the Atacama before turning to fiction. She writes quiet, character-driven science fiction about people who talk to things that may not be listening.

chapters.title: The Beacon Nobody Ordered
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. On the anniversary of the colony's founding, Rosalind performs her solitary maintenance ritual on the beacon, cataloguing its impossible age and the paperwork trail that ends in nothing. A young archivist, Teo, asks why she stays. She deflects; privately, she admits she stays because the beacon is the only thing that still speaks her language. Beat: loneliness disguised as duty.

chapters.title: Children of One Sleep
chapters.summary: POV alternating Rosalind and Wren, a twelve-year-old. Fourteen children wake having dreamed the same dream: a corridor of light folding like paper, and a voice counting down in no language anyone knows — except Rosalind, who recognizes the phoneme structure from the beacon's transmissions. The colony council dismisses it as mass hysteria. Beat: dread arriving quietly, in daylight.

chapters.title: Grammar of the Deep
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Working nights with Wren's dream drawings, Rosalind decodes the first true sentence: 'the window opens once.' The syntax is human-adjacent, built from her own published papers — someone out there learned to speak by reading her. Her hands shake. Teo catches her burning her notes and covers for her without asking why. Beat: the thrill and terror of being addressed across the dark.

chapters.title: What the Council Knows
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Digging into sealed colonial records, Rosalind finds her own immigration file falsified: she was recruited, not stranded, and the beacon was commissioned the year before she arrived. Confronting Administrator Okafor, she is told the truth would panic the colony and that the children must be kept away from her. Beat: loyalty begins to crack against the weight of what she wasn't told.

chapters.title: The Dream Spreads
chapters.summary: POV Wren. The dream jumps to adults — then to everyone who sleeps within earshot of the beacon. The countdown accelerates. Wren, half in love with the dream's beauty, defends it against frightened parents; Rosalind realizes the signal isn't attacking, it's teaching, and the colony is failing every lesson. Beat: fear curdling into division, with Wren as its fault line.

chapters.title: Dead Space
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The relay at the edge of dead space is the only transmitter powerful enough to answer the signal properly — and the jump window for reaching it closes in eleven days. Okafor forbids the trip; Rosalind steals a skiff anyway, taking Wren along because the child is the best translator she has. Teo chooses to come. Beat: the point of no return, chosen freely.

chapters.title: Eleven Days of Silence
chapters.summary: POV Teo. The crossing through dead space, where comms die and the dream follows them into sleep. Teo narrates the fragile found-family forming aboard the skiff — shared meals, Wren's nightmares soothed by Rosalind's invented lullabies in the alien grammar. They learn the countdown matches the jump window exactly. Beat: tenderness under pressure; love becoming a reason to go back.

chapters.title: The Relay Speaks
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. At the relay, Rosalind finds logs proving the beacon was built to call something home — something that left before humanity arrived, and chose her, years ago, as its voice. The final message resolves: answer truly, or the window shuts and the signal turns inward, into the dreamers. Beat: revelation as betrayal; the price of survival made explicit.

chapters.title: Answer in Her Own Voice
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. With minutes left, Rosalind refuses the scripted reply the signal offers and answers in her own words — admitting fear, claiming the colony as hers, offering truth instead of obedience. Wren adds a line of pure child-logic that completes the grammar. The countdown stops. The window begins closing with them on the wrong side of it. Beat: climax — honesty as the only winning move.

chapters.title: Hazel and the Archive
chapters.summary: POV Wren, months later. The skiff limps home through a reopened secondary route the answering presence cleared for them. The dreams are gone, but Wren keeps a dream of her own now: a garden-archive where the voice waits, patient, for whoever comes next. Rosalind plants hazel trees by the beacon and finally sleeps in two languages at once. Beat: resolution — belonging earned, not given.
